subject: Philosophy
question_text: Who is widely regarded as the founder of classical utilitarianism in modern philosophy?
explanation_detailed: Jeremy Bentham developed utilitarianism as a systematic moral theory based on maximizing pleasure and minimizing pain. Kant and Aristotle belong to deontological and virtue traditions, not utilitarianism.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Immanuel Kant's central moral command, requiring us to act only on maxims we could will as universal laws, is called the:
explanation_detailed: Kant's categorical imperative binds us unconditionally, regardless of personal desires. A hypothetical imperative applies only if we want a particular end, which is not Kant's main moral standard.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Rule utilitarianism differs from act utilitarianism because rule utilitarianism:
option_c: Treats duty as more important than happiness
option_d: Judges actions by following rules that generally maximize utility
explanation_detailed: Rule utilitarians ask whether obeying a rule tends to produce the best overall results, even when a single act might seem to bring more benefit. Act utilitarianism evaluates each action directly by its consequences.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Bentham's method for measuring pleasure and pain by factors such as intensity, duration, and certainty is known as the:
explanation_detailed: Bentham used the hedonic calculus to compare pleasures and pains in a practical way. The categorical test belongs to Kant, while the veil of ignorance is linked to John Rawls.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: According to Kant, the only thing good without qualification is:
explanation_detailed: Kant argued that a good will, acting from duty and respect for moral law, has unconditional moral worth. Happiness and pleasure may be desirable, but they are not morally good in every case.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Utilitarianism is best classified as a form of:
explanation_detailed: Utilitarianism judges right and wrong by the consequences of actions, especially their effect on overall welfare. Virtue ethics focuses on character, not primarily on outcomes.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Deontological ethics primarily evaluates actions by:
option_d: Whether they fulfill moral duty and respect persons as ends
explanation_detailed: Deontology holds that some actions are wrong even if they produce good results, because duty and respect for persons matter morally. Utilitarianism, by contrast, focuses on maximizing welfare.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: John Stuart Mill argued that the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is:
explanation_detailed: Mill's harm principle limits coercion to cases where one person's conduct injures others. He rejected paternalistic interference merely to make a person happier or more virtuous.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Kant's test of universalizability asks whether we could consistently will that:
option_a: Everyone follow the same maxim in similar situations
option_b: Only rulers should obey moral law
option_d: Tradition should decide every moral question
explanation_detailed: If a maxim cannot be universalized without contradiction or unacceptable results, Kant treats the action as morally impermissible. This test checks the form of the rule, not merely its consequences.

subject: Philosophy
question_text: Mill distinguished higher pleasures from lower pleasures by saying that:
option_c: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied
option_d: All pleasures are morally equal in every respect
explanation_detailed: Mill argued that intellectual and moral pleasures are qualitatively superior to merely bodily pleasures. Bentham had treated pleasures more as quantities to be added together.
